metadata.title: Understanding Filipino students’ achievement in PISA: The roles of personal characteristics, proximal processes, and social contexts

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used the publicly available Philippines PISA 2018 microdata, which already includes weights to account for PISA’s complex two-stage sampling (schools first, then students within schools). The authors explicitly state that they used these published weights for classical statistical inferences and, for the hierarchical linear modeling step, they used the 80 replicate weights included in the dataset. For the Random Forest step, they did not use replicate weights because the RF procedure does not generate parameter estimates in the same way as survey-weighted regression. The analytic sample was restricted by variable-exclusion rules (dropping variables with 100% missingness, removing redundant ESCS components, and excluding predictors not significantly correlated with reading), and missing values were handled via multiple imputation before model training.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Philippines PISA 2018 dataset (15-year-olds; N=7233). Sampling followed PISA’s complex two-stage design (about 187 schools sampled across the Philippines, then students sampled within schools). For predictors, the authors excluded variables with 100% missingness, removed ESCS sub-indices used to derive ESCS to avoid redundancy, and removed variables that did not show a statistically significant correlation with reading achievement in preliminary analysis, reducing the predictor set to 53 variables. For missing data, they assessed missingness with an 80% missingness threshold per case; all 7223 observations had <25% missingness and were retained. They then performed multiple imputation using MICE (mice package in R) before the primary ML and HLM analyses.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (Model 2, top 26 predictors): R²=0.64; RMSE=47.50 (unobserved sample). Model 1 (all 53 predictors): R²=0.66; RMSE=47.19. Cross-validation selected 26 predictors as optimal (lowest error rate RMSE=47.75 at 26 predictors).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (Philippines; 15-year-olds) the study leveraged reading difficulty self-concept (SCREADDIFF), socioeconomic status (ESCS), grade repetition (REPEAT), school belongingness (BELONG), and time spent on online reading (ST176) to predict reading achievement (PVREAD1–PVREAD10), finding that the most critical predictors were dominated by personal characteristics, proximal processes, and contextual factors, with SCREADDIFF showing the highest impact and ESCS/REPEAT/BELONG emerging as key contextual predictors. This indicates that Philippine reading improvement strategies should simultaneously target students’ reading self-beliefs, learning opportunities (especially online reading time), and school-level socioeconomic and climate conditions, while noting that the evidence is predictive (not causal) and based on cross-sectional PISA data.

data.outcome_summary: The study used the Philippines’ first-time PISA 2018 microdata (N=7233, 15-year-olds) with reading literacy as the outcome, operationalized via 10 plausible values (PVREAD1–PVREAD10) aggregated following PISA procedures. After excluding redundant and non-informative predictors, the authors trained a Random Forest regression model in two stages: Model 1 with 53 predictors and Model 2 streamlined to the empirically selected top 26 predictors via repeated 10-fold cross-validation. For Model 2, the Random Forest explained about 64% of variance in the unobserved sample (R²=0.64) with RMSE≈47.50; Model 1 achieved R²=0.66 (RMSE≈47.19), indicating only a minimal loss in predictive power. The most important predictors included reading difficulty self-concept, ESCS, grade repetition, school belongingness, and fixed mindset, with HLM providing broadly similar but not identical effect patterns. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and the fact that Random Forest variable importance is predictive rather than causal.
